lines.text: Imagine you're stocking a giant industrial freezer... when the door slams shut behind you.
It's minus twenty degrees Celsius, and fans keep blasting frozen air across your body.
You push the door. It won't budge.
Within seconds, you feel cold. But that's just nerves in your skin sounding the alarm. Your core is still a normal thirty-seven degrees.
To protect it, your body squeezes the blood vessels in your skin, pulling warm blood away from your hands.
Then the shivering starts: rapid muscle twitches that burn energy to make heat.
But heat is escaping everywhere: into the air, out with every breath, and into anything you touch.
Your fingers go numb and clumsy. And the thick metal walls block your signal.
Then you remember: most freezers have an emergency release inside the door.
But this one is jammed with ice.
You hurry to break it free... and the frosted floor takes your legs out.
Hours can pass. Your core slowly cools, and below thirty-five degrees, you have hypothermia.
In this mild stage, you shiver violently. Your hands fumble, your speech slurs, and your judgment starts to slip.
Your best move: get off the metal floor, which pulls heat out of you. Sit on cardboard, tuck your hands into your armpits, and curl up.
Nearing thirty-two degrees, something frightening can happen: the shivering stops. Not because you're warm, but because your body is running out of ways to fight.
Confusion and drowsiness creep in. You might not even realize you're in danger.
Below about twenty-eight, people usually lose consciousness, and the heart's rhythm can turn dangerously unstable.
So... could you survive?
In cold air, serious hypothermia usually takes hours, not minutes. But there's no fixed countdown.
It depends on the temperature, moving air, your clothing, staying dry, your body and health... and how fast you're found.
Feeling cold is your body's alarm. Hypothermia is when that alarm goes quiet.
Doctors have even revived people from astonishingly low temperatures. As they say: nobody's dead until they're warm and dead.
